result: The tumor microenvironment (TME) is a complex, heterogeneous ecosystem composed of multiple cell types, proteins, and soluble factors that varies by anatomic site and influences critical cancer phenotypes including initiation, metastasis, and drug resistance, which are major causes of cancer mortality.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C8-C12) establish foundational knowledge about the TME that is well-supported by established cancer biology principles and cited literature. The claims are consistent with current understanding of cancer as an ecosystem and provide appropriate context for the review's focus on zebrafish models.

result: Current model systems for studying the TME have significant limitations: mice are challenging for large-scale TME perturbation and single-cell imaging despite their advantages, while organoids are limited to studying one or two TME cell types.
evaluation: Claims C13-C18 accurately describe the limitations of existing models based on established knowledge and cited literature. The practical constraints of mouse breeding for TME studies and the limited complexity of organoid systems are well-documented challenges in the field.

result: Zebrafish share substantial genetic conservation with humans (70% genome, >80% disease genes) and possess most TME components, while offering major advantages in genetic manipulation at scale and in vivo imaging capabilities.
evaluation: Claims C19-C23 and C34 are well-supported by the cited reference (Patton et al., 2021) and established zebrafish literature. The genetic conservation statistics and technical advantages are consistent with the zebrafish research community's understanding of the model system.

result: Cell-type-specific promoters in zebrafish have been successfully used to model cancer, including the rag2 promoter driving MYC to generate T-cell leukemia and the mitfa promoter driving BRAFV600E to generate melanoma, with subsequent applications for modifier screens and CRISPR-based gene inactivation.
evaluation: Claims C24-C29 describe established zebrafish cancer models supported by multiple citations (Langenau et al., 2003; Patton et al., 2005; Ceol et al., 2011; Kaufman et al., 2016; Venkatesan et al., 2018; Ablain et al., 2018). These represent foundational work in zebrafish cancer modeling.

result: Zebrafish support tumor cell transplantation at both larval/embryonic stages (prior to adaptive immunity development) and adult stages (requiring immunocompromise), using either zebrafish-derived or human-derived cell lines.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 describe well-established transplantation methodologies in zebrafish, supported by cited literature (Heilmann et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2019) and general knowledge about zebrafish immune development.

result: Zebrafish enable whole-animal imaging at single-cell resolution due to their small size and optical transparency, allowing investigation of all metastatic steps (intravasation, circulation, extravasation, outgrowth) within a single animal.
evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by cited literature (Singleman and Holtzman, 2014; Loveless et al., 2020; Gupta and Massagué, 2006) and logical inference from zebrafish physical properties. The ability to image entire metastatic cascades is a unique advantage of the model.

result: Spatial transcriptomics in zebrafish melanoma models identified a distinct 'interface' cell state in tumor and TME cells at physical contact sites, characterized by upregulation of cilia genes.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 describe specific findings from Hunter et al., 2021, demonstrating the application of spatial transcriptomics to zebrafish cancer models. The identification of interface cell states represents a concrete discovery enabled by the zebrafish system.

result: Zebrafish offer superior scalability compared to mice, with the ability to work with hundreds to thousands of animals, placement in 96-well plates for screening, and breeding pairs yielding hundreds versus approximately a dozen offspring.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47 accurately describe practical advantages of zebrafish based on established knowledge and cited literature (Patton et al., 2021). The numerical comparisons are consistent with standard breeding outcomes for both species.

result: Larval xenograft assays in zebrafish have revealed multiple TME mechanisms including RhoC-mediated vascular opening via VEGF secretion, macrophage requirement for tumor angiogenesis, and differential TME generation by patient-matched cancer cells through immune cell recruitment.
evaluation: Claims C48-C57 describe established larval xenograft methodologies and specific findings supported by multiple citations (Hoeppner et al., 2015; Rebelo de Almeida et al., 2020; Pekkonen et al., 2018; Britto et al., 2018; Fazio et al., 2020; Fior et al., 2017; Póvoa et al., 2021). These represent validated applications of the model.

result: Transgenic zebrafish cancer models at early developmental stages have identified pro-tumoral roles of innate immunity including neutrophil recruitment, basement membrane breaching, and leukocyte-derived PGE2, though adaptive immunity and stromal cells are absent in embryos.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by multiple citations (Antonio et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2012, 2010; van den Berg et al., 2019; Minchin and Rawls, 2017; Page et al., 2013; Trede et al., 2004). The limitation regarding adaptive immunity is appropriately acknowledged.

result: The casper zebrafish strain enables adult imaging and has been used to identify endothelin signaling requirements in melanoma dissemination and to test drug efficacy in immunocompromised xenograft models.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 describe the casper strain and its applications, supported by citations (White et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2019). The development and application of this strain represents an important technical advance for adult zebrafish studies.

result: Continuous live imaging in zebrafish revealed cooperative metastatic behavior of tumor cell clusters with distinct invasive and proliferative states regulated by TFAP2, and identified hemodynamic flow effects on extravasation.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 describe specific imaging-based discoveries supported by citations (Stoletov et al., 2007; Campbell et al., 2021; Follain et al., 2018). These findings demonstrate the power of continuous imaging in zebrafish for understanding metastatic mechanisms.

result: Normal resident cells in the TME (keratinocytes, fibroblasts, adipocytes) undergo bidirectional reprogramming with tumor cells, with fibroblasts becoming cancer-associated fibroblasts and macrophages becoming tumor-associated macrophages through mechanisms including LIF and Vitamin D signaling.
evaluation: Claims C72-C79 describe established TME biology supported by multiple citations (Golan et al., 2015; Kaur et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Sahai et al., 2020; Quail and Joyce, 2017; Albrengues et al., 2015; Sherman et al., 2014). This provides important biological context for TME studies.

result: Zebrafish possess an extensive collection of cell-type-specific promoters/enhancers for TME cells including skin (mitfa, krt4, tp63, plin2), immune (cd79, lck/rag2, mpeg1), and vascular (fli1a) cells, with ~140,000 cis-regulatory regions cataloged by DANIO-CODE.
evaluation: Claims C4, C80-C89 describe the promoter/enhancer toolbox supported by numerous citations and the DANIO-CODE consortium data (Baranasic et al., 2022). This comprehensive resource is a key strength of the zebrafish system for TME studies, though the manuscript notes some cell types (e.g., NK cells) lack specific promoters.

result: Random insertional screens can identify promoters for rare cell types, as demonstrated by identification of neuronal subpopulations essential for fear conditioning.
evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by citation to Lal et al., 2018 and describes a valid approach for expanding the promoter toolkit, though this is a single example rather than systematic validation of the approach for TME studies.

result: Zebrafish have anatomical differences from humans (gills vs lungs, no lymph nodes, kidney marrow vs bone marrow) that limit modeling of certain metastatic sites, though gills share cell types with lungs and alternative approaches exist for studying lymphangiogenesis and bone marrow metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C91-C99 appropriately acknowledge important limitations of the zebrafish model while noting partial conservation and alternative approaches, supported by multiple citations (Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011; Cadiz and Jonz, 2020; Lin et al., 2020; Astin et al., 2014; Paul et al., 2019; Sacco et al., 2016). This balanced assessment is important for the review.

result: CRISPR has been successfully adapted for cell-type-specific gene editing in zebrafish using tissue-specific promoters to drive Cas9, with applications including the MASERATI system for melanocyte-specific knockout and anti-CRISPR for enhanced specificity, plus ablation systems for entire cell types.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C100-C107 describe CRISPR methodologies supported by multiple citations (Hwang et al., 2013; Burger et al., 2016; Ablain and Zon, 2016; Ablain et al., 2015, 2018; Isiaku et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2019; Curado et al., 2008; Pisharath et al., 2007; Wan et al., 2006). These tools are essential for TME perturbation studies.

result: Conditional and inducible systems exist in zebrafish including ERT2-GAL4, GAL4-EcR, LexPR, TET, and Cre-controlled CRISPR (3C), though these are less reliable than in mice and not commonly used.
evaluation: Claims C108-C114 describe available conditional systems supported by citations (Akerberg et al., 2014; Esengil et al., 2007; Emelyanov and Parinov, 2008; Knopf et al., 2010; Hans et al., 2021), while appropriately noting their limitations (C112). This honest assessment of technical challenges is important.

result: Non-germline approaches including F0 crispants and TEAZ enable rapid, scalable genetic studies in zebrafish, achieving >90% phenotype penetrance with multiple sgRNAs and allowing simultaneous use of up to seven constructs, with applications including identification of GRAMD1B as a metastasis suppressor.
evaluation: Claims C115-C121 describe non-germline methodologies supported by multiple citations (Burger et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018; Ceol et al., 2011; Weiss et al., 2022; Ablain et al., 2018; Callahan et al., 2018; Suresh et al., 2022). These approaches address scalability challenges and represent important technical advances.

result: Lineage tracing technologies including Cre-lox, Brainbow, zebrabow, scGESTALT, and LINNAEUS enable tracking of TME cell reprogramming, with scGESTALT/LINNAEUS first implemented in zebrafish and offering advantages in temporal resolution and scalability.
evaluation: Claims C122-C127 describe lineage tracing approaches supported by multiple citations (Wagner and Klein, 2020; Livet et al., 2007; Mosimann et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2013; Raj et al., 2018; Spanjaard et al., 2018). The development of these technologies in zebrafish demonstrates the model's utility for complex biological questions.

result: Novel cell-cell interaction technologies including SynNotch, LIPSTIC, mCherry-Niche, and G-baToN can be adapted to zebrafish to systematically identify and characterize heterotypic tumor-TME interactions.
evaluation: Claims C128-C132 describe technologies developed in mice (Hou et al., 2021; Pasqual et al., 2018; Ombrato et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020) with one zebrafish application (Wang et al., 2021 for SynNotch). While the authors state these 'could be adapted' to zebrafish, most lack demonstrated implementation, making this more of a proposal than an established result.

result: Heterotypic cell-cell interactions between tumor and TME cells contribute to tumorigenic phenotypes through mechanisms including adherens junctions, contact-dependent migration, protease expression, perivascular niche signaling, and fatty acid transfer from adipocytes.
evaluation: Claims C133-C139 describe established mechanisms of tumor-TME interaction supported by multiple citations (Cavey and Lecuit, 2009; Barone et al., 2017; Dumortier et al., 2012; Breznik et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2018). This provides biological context for why studying these interactions in zebrafish is important.

result: Zebrafish models show differential metastatic capacity (xenografts/allografts readily metastasize while transgenics do not), likely due to technical limitations and genetic complexity requirements, though the model enables imaging of all metastatic steps and investigation of TME factors regulating each step.
evaluation: Claims C140-C147 provide an honest assessment of metastasis modeling in zebrafish, acknowledging limitations (C140-C142) while describing capabilities for studying metastatic mechanisms, supported by citations (Lawson and Weinstein, 2002; Hung et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2016; Langenau et al., 2004; Ellett et al., 2011; Valiente et al., 2014). This balanced perspective is important.

result: Transgenic zebrafish approaches may better model organ tropism than transplantation-based methods in mice, as they allow metastasis to occur gradually and more closely recapitulate patient disease progression.
evaluation: Claims C148-C150 compare approaches across species, with C148-C149 describing established mouse methods (van der Weyden et al., 2017) but C150 making a speculative claim about zebrafish advantages ('likely more closely recapitulates') without direct comparative data. This is more hypothesis than demonstrated result.

result: Zebrafish immune studies face challenges due to limited antibody cross-reactivity, but transgenic lines marking immune cell types (CD4+ T-regs, T cells, B-cells, macrophages, neutrophils) are available, though it remains unknown whether zebrafish immune responses to neoantigens match mammalian models.
evaluation: Claims C151-C156 honestly assess both capabilities and limitations of zebrafish immunology, supported by citations (Moore et al., 2016; Kasheta et al., 2017; Langenau et al., 2003; Burroughs-Garcia et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2017; Gray et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2021). The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C156) is appropriate.

result: TME-mediated drug resistance in melanoma occurs through multiple mechanisms including stromal HGF secretion and aged fibroblast fatty acid secretion, with FATP inhibition overcoming resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C157-C161 describe established mechanisms of TME-mediated resistance supported by citations (Straussman et al., 2012; Alicea et al., 2020). These provide important biological context for why zebrafish TME studies could inform therapeutic development.

result: Zebrafish enable high-throughput chemical screening in whole animals, with embryos/larvae particularly suited for 96-well format screening, leading to clinical translation of compounds like ProHema (Phase II) and olaparib plus temozolomide (Phase I), though most screens have targeted tumor cells rather than the TME.
evaluation: Claims C162-C168 describe screening capabilities and clinical successes supported by citations (Letrado et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; North et al., 2007; Goessling et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2019; Dang et al., 2016; Lu and Patton, 2022; Pugach et al., 2009), while appropriately noting the gap in TME-focused screening (C167).

result: Drug activity shows some species specificity between zebrafish and humans, though zebrafish can more effectively predict certain drug toxicities (e.g., thalidomide) compared to mouse models.
evaluation: Claims C169-C170 appropriately acknowledge both conservation and differences in drug responses, supported by citations (Asnake et al., 2019; Letrado et al., 2018; Patton et al., 2021). This balanced assessment is important for interpreting zebrafish drug screening results.
